# Results — Study 275 (Whisky-Cask) vs the S&P 500 (^GSPC)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The annual rare-whisky /
cask index is hardcoded in [`data.py`](../whisky_cask/data.py) (appraisal-based,
rebased 100 @ 2008, price-only). S&P 500 calendar-year **price** returns are computed
from the repo-level cache `_cache/^GSPC_split_only.parquet` (December/December close).
Match the fingerprint below to confirm you hold the same data. As-of **2026-06-17**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n observations | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| Whisky index (appraisal-based, annual) | 2009–2024 returns | 16 years | `925a321f826e` |
| S&P 500 ^GSPC (price-only, Dec/Dec) | 2009–2024 | 16 years | (paired) |

Both legs are **price-only**: the whisky index has no income, so S&P dividends are
stripped to keep the comparison apples-to-apples on the Signal axis. The
**total-return** S&P would beat whisky outright (noted under *Could you trade it?*).

## Raw performance — the seductive headline

| Metric | Whisky | S&P 500 |
|---|--:|--:|
| Annualised return | **+12.17%** | +12.42% |
| Volatility (reported) | **10.21%** | 13.92% |
| Naive Sharpe (rf=2%) | **1.04** | 0.81 |
| Correlation to S&P | **−0.17** | 1.00 |

At face value this is the perfect alt-asset pitch: a similar return at lower
volatility (hence a higher Sharpe) with a near-zero, even *negative*, correlation
to equities. Whisky beat the S&P in only **56%** of years, though — a coin flip.

## The appraisal-smoothing trap (the killer) — Geltner (1991) unsmoothing

The reported series has a **lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.779** — a value impossible
for a genuine, transaction-based asset return (those are near white noise) and the
unmistakable fingerprint of an appraisal-based index that anchors each year's mark to
the previous one. Undo it:

| Metric | Reported (smoothed) | Unsmoothed (true est.) |
|---|--:|--:|
| Volatility | 10.21% | **29.13%** (×2.85) |
| Naive Sharpe | 1.04 | **0.25** |

The "low-vol alternative asset" is, measured honestly, **more volatile than the
S&P** (29% vs 14%), and its Sharpe collapses from 1.04 to **0.25** — below a passive
equity index fund. The entire risk-adjusted edge was a measurement artifact.

## The cost wedge (the second killer)

The index is the price realised by a *seller of the rarest bottles at auction*. A
retail cask buyer pays frictions the index never sees:

| Friction | Assumption |
|---|--:|
| Entry dealer markup (amortised) | 40% |
| Storage + insurance | 1.5%/yr |
| Angels' Share (evaporation) | 2.0%/yr |
| Exit commission | 10% |

| | Annualised |
|---|--:|
| Index (gross) | +12.17% |
| Cask owner (net of all costs) | **+5.93%** |
| Cost wedge | **−6.24pp/yr** |

Net of costs the cask owner keeps roughly **half** the index — and falls behind even
price-only equities, let alone total-return equities.

## Inference — HAC excess-return test (whisky − S&P)

H0: whisky does not beat the S&P per year.

| Metric | Value |
|---|--:|
| Mean annual excess (whisky − S&P) | **−0.67pp** |
| HAC (Newey-West, 1 lag) t-stat | **−0.15** |
| Whisky-wins fraction | 56% |

The point estimate of the "edge" is **negative**, with |t| ≈ 0.15 — nowhere near the
|t| ≥ 2 bar a `REAL` signal demands. And with only **n = 16** annual observations,
the test has essentially no power to certify an edge even if one existed.

## Honesty checks

- **Execution lag.** Appraisal indices are reported *in arrears* (a year-Y level is
  published in early Y+1). A buyer cannot transact on a mark they only learn months
  later — a structural tradability problem, separate from costs.
- **Costs one-way × NAV.** Entry markup and exit commission are charged on the full
  position value; recurring storage/insurance/evaporation are subtracted each year.
  No leverage, no shorts (you cannot short a cask), so no borrow.
- **Gross/net and price-only/total-return labeled.** Both legs are price-only; the
  whisky figures are gross unless tagged "net"; the S&P here excludes dividends, which
  *flatters* whisky — the honest (total-return) comparison is even worse for casks.
- **Survivorship (Signal axis).** The index is a curated basket of the *rarest,
  most sought-after* bottles — exactly the survivors. Distilleries and casks that
  failed or never appreciated never enter the index, biasing the headline return up.
  An individual cask is far more likely to track the losers than the index.

## Could you trade it?

There is no cask ETF, no daily NAV, no two-sided market. Entry is via brokers at
opaque markups; exit is via auction at commission, often months later; the asset is
physical, perishable (evaporating), and storage-bound. The honest benchmark — a
total-return global index fund — wins on **return, liquidity, and cost simultaneously**.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** Mean annual excess −0.7pp, HAC t = −0.15. The headline Sharpe
  (1.04) is a smoothing artifact that collapses to 0.25 once the index is unsmoothed;
  the unsmoothed volatility (29%) exceeds equities. No robust |t| ≥ 2 anywhere; n = 16
  has no power regardless.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** No tradable vehicle; a ~6.2pp/yr cost wedge cuts ~12%
  gross to ~6% net; the index is appraisal-based, price-only, illiquid, reported in
  arrears, and survivorship-curated — unreachable by any actual buyer.
- **Busted — an appraisal mirage in a bottle.** The three-part pitch (uncorrelated,
  low-vol, equity-beating) fails on all three: the low vol is measurement smoothing,
  the return ties (and loses net), and the negative correlation is sign noise at n=16.
